entities.title: Keep raw BSD syscalls on macOS?
entities.summary: On macOS the invoker links libSystem anyway, but still makes its I/O, socket and exec calls as raw BSD syscalls, an interface its own header calls unsupported by Apple and a spike.
entities.context: sys_darwin_arm64.h issues read, write, open, close, socket, connect, sendmsg, recvmsg, getsockopt, getuid, execve and exit through `svc #0x80` with hard-coded syscall numbers and the carry-flag error convention; its header says "the BSD syscall ABI is unsupported by Apple, so the spike measures it". Since a freestanding Mach-O is killed on exec (macos/c/zazzle/.dev/decisions.json, why-not-freestanding-on-macos), the program links libSystem and already calls its _NSGetExecutablePath, nanosleep and posix_spawn. Whether the raw calls are meant to stay once the spike has been measured is not written down; since then the non-blocking receive for the spin and the execve for the standalone tools, run and proxy have been added as raw calls too.

options.title: Keep the raw syscalls
options.consequences: One code path shape on both platforms; relies on syscall numbers and conventions Apple does not promise to keep, so a macOS update could break zazzle there.

options.title: Call libSystem's wrappers on macOS
options.consequences: Uses Apple's supported interface at no extra linking cost; the macOS backend no longer exercises the raw path, and the Linux and macOS backends differ more.

origin.by: Coding agent documenting the invoker for HASD

entities.title: Spin briefly before blocking on the reply
entities.summary: The invoker polls for the daemon's status byte without sleeping for up to 25 µs before it blocks on the read.
entities.context: Many daemon commands (a read of a cached file) finish in microseconds, and putting the invoker to sleep on the socket and waking it again costs about as much as the work itself.

options.title: Block on the read at once
options.consequences: No wasted CPU, but every fast reply pays a sleep and a wake-up.

options.title: Poll for a short, fixed time, then block
options.consequences: Fast replies skip the sleep and wake-up; slow commands lose at most the spin time of CPU.

entities.decision: read_status polls with a non-blocking one-byte recvmsg for up to SPIN_US (25 µs), timed with CNTVCT_EL0 on arm64 and clock_gettime on x86_64 and with a pause or yield hint between polls, then falls back to a blocking read. An error other than would-block ends the spin at once.
entities.rationale: Per the README and the commit that introduced it, fast replies skip a sleep and wake-up that cost about as much as the daemon's work on a Linux VM, and slow commands lose at most 25 µs of CPU; the readings are in the README.

origin.reference: macos/c/zazzle/README.md, section What it does (rationale moved here); commit 2bb253d
